items.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025
items.q: When you were working with Gamble and Huff and Thom Bell... I got more and more accepted into it. You know Kenny Gamble... he used to come to my studio... his son came and worked for me

ctx.x: Yeah and they wouldn't even have to play it again, we'll just like move it over there. When you were working with Gamble and Huff and Thom Bell, I'm trying to frame this idea. Before someone coined the term the Philly Sound, was there a speculation or conversations about what is Motown not doing that we could do? How can we find a niche in the market?

You know I think the big difference between Motown and Philly Sound was Motown was the sound of the young America. It was really a youth movement. R&B. Whereas the Philly sound was a sophisticated, much jazzier much more adult kind of a sound. I mean I've always thought that MFSB could have been the Lionel Hampton band. You know? And in turn, in a way, I was right. MFSB could have gone and played behind Frank Sinatra or anybody. You know? I mean it was that adept at a lot of different styles and adult styles. And…

mean I think Tommy Bell was enamored with Burt Bacharach. And Burt Bacharach was very sophisticated you know? And I think a lot of Thom's arrangements back in those days were like Bacharach arrangements. They would feature a horn player or feature a flute or feature — I mean feature a harp. I mean he had his way of introducing symphonic instruments. And in the '70s, early '70s, that was a big deal I think.

items.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025
items.q: I would wait for Tommy Bell to smile or Gamble & Huff to say damn that's nice or McFadden and Whitehead to come in and start dancing in the studio in front of the strings.

ctx.x: I read a quote from let's see, who said it — Fred Wesley, when I spoke to him. He said this phrase probably six times in the interview talking about writing for James Brown he said, "I didn't know what I was doing." And he kept saying it, like — and I felt like saying, "Well yes you did." But have you ever been in a situation early on that you didn't feel like you knew what you were doing?

Absolutely. You learn on the job. That's what Fred means. But Fred was a great player. And he knew all about that stuff, he had grown up listening to those records. Come on. You know? But yeah I mean my early on I would look for — I would wait for Tommy Bell to smile or Gamble & Huff to say damn that's nice or McFadden and Whitehead to come in and start dancing in the studio in front of the strings. You know? All of a sudden I said, "I take it you like it." They said, "Yeah we do." I mean Whitehead used to call…
Well you had no issues being accepted into that if it was a circle, but I'll call it a circle?
